headline: A wallet is “wealth” plus “cloth” — a Japanese coinage found in texts from 1675.

sources.quote: Appears to be a Japanese coinage based on Middle Chinese-derived roots, as a compound of 財 (sai, “wealth, money”) + 布 (fu, “cloth [pouch]”). Found in texts starting from 1675.

headline: “Cold” may be “claw” plus “painful”, with a missing i.

sources.quote: Compound of 爪 (tsume, “claw”) + 痛い (itai, “painful”), with the medial /-i-/ falling out.

headline: Hydrogen is “water element” — a word-for-word copy of Dutch, coined in 1834.

sources.quote: Calque of Dutch waterstof (literally “waterstuff”), equivalent to 水 (sui, “water”) + 素 (so, “element”). Compare German Wasserstoff, Luxembourgish Waasserstoff.
Coined by Japanese scientist Udagawa Yōan in 1834 in his book 遠西医方名物考補遺 (“水素”).

headline: The youngest child is the “end child” — with a little clipped-off pause in the middle.

sources.quote: Shift from earlier 末(すえ)子(こ) (sueko), from 末 (sue, “end”) + 子 (ko, “child”).

headline: The word for an aunt is a “little mother” — and the kanji don't spell it that way.

sources.quote: From 小 (o, “little”) + 母 (ha, “mother”). The kanji is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)). Compare 小母 (oba).

headline: A human being is, in Chinese, “people” plus “among”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 人間 (MC nyin kean|keanH). Analyzable as a compound of "people" + "among; space".

First cited to a text from 984. The kanji spelling is cited earlier in a kanbun passage in the Shoku Nihongi of 756, listed in some references with the reading jinkan. However, the extant copies of this work that include phonetic guides are centuries younger than this first date, raising the possibility that the ningen reading might itself date from 756.

meaning: to refuse, to decline, to dismiss
headline: To refuse was originally to “split words”.

sources.quote: Originally a compound of 言 (koto, “words”) + 割る (waru, “split”).

headline: A doll is a “person shape”, and a native reading, built from hito and kata, says the same thing.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 人形 (nyin heng, literally “person shape”).

headline: A meal, or cooked rice, with an honorific on the front.

sources.quote: Compound of 御 (go-, honorific prefix) + 飯 (han, “cooked rice”).

headline: “Quiet” is a bound root meaning “quietness”, plus a か that makes na-adjectives.

sources.quote: Compound of 静 (shizu, bound morpheme indicating “quietness” or “calmness”) + か (-ka, suffixing element used to form na adjectives). The shizu portion is cognate with the shizu in 静まる (shizumaru, “to become quiet”) and 沈む (shizumu, “to sink; to set (such as the sun or moon); to become depressed”). This shizu might also be related to 下 (shita, “down; below”).
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: The usual reading of “disciple”, でし, is a shift from the older Chinese-derived ていし.

sources.quote: Appears to be a shift from teishi above. This is now the most common reading for the disciple, apprentice sense.

headline: Three days out has its own word, and nobody is sure what its first syllable is.

sources.quote: Compound of し (shi, of uncertain derivation) + 明後日 (asatte, “the day after tomorrow”).
The initial shi element is uncertain. Speculatively, this might be related to, or a shift from, intensifying prefix ひ (hi) found in some adjectives, such as ひ弱(よわ)い (hiyowai, “delicate, very weak”).
First cited to a text from 1275.

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: An autograph, a sign and a sine all land on one katakana spelling.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English sine.
Borrowed from English sign.

headline: A “beautiful person” has a native twin spelled the same way: “good-faced person”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 美人 (MC mijX nyin, literally “beautiful (especially feminine) + person”). Compare modern Min Nan reading bí-jîn.
The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing.

meaning: to be grounded on, to be based on
headline: To be based on something is to “attach” to a “foundation”.

sources.quote: From 基(もと) (moto, “base, foundation”) + 付(つ)く (tsuku). The tsuku changes to zuku as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: “Freedom” is an old Chinese word that Fukuzawa Yukichi repurposed in the 1860s.

sources.quote: /d͡ʑiːu/ → /d͡ʑijuː/

Apparently first imported from Middle Chinese 自由 (MC dzijH yuw) with an original meaning of roughly “arising from oneself”. Repurposed in the 1860s by Fukuzawa Yukichi as a translation of English freedom or liberty, as an extension of the original meaning: “freedom to act according to one's own thoughts, without restriction”. However, Li (2014) proposes that since the Han dynasty 自由 already meant “to be free”, from earlier “to follow oneself.”

headline: “Tonight” was /kʲəm bʉan/ in its Chinese-derived reading, and became /kombaɴ/.

sources.quote: */kʲəm bʉan/ → /kombaɴ/
From Middle Chinese compound 今晚 (MC kim mjonX).

headline: “Interesting” is literally “face-white”, with cousins in Okinawan and Miyako.

sources.quote: From 面 (omo, “face”) + 白い (shiroi, “white”).
Cognate with Okinawan うむっさん (umussan) and Miyako うむっし (umusshi).

headline: The “Messrs.” you write on a company envelope is an honorific stuck on the word for “inside”.

sources.quote: Compound of 御 (on-, honorific prefix) + 中 (chū, “inside; middle”).

headline: Good night is a polite “rest” — and the verb for rest began as an adjective meaning “easy”.

sources.quote: Compound of 御(お) (o-, honorific prefix) + 休(やす)み (yasumi, “rest, a break, a holiday”), the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 休(やす)む (yasumu), itself from adjective 安(やす)い (yasui, “easygoing; easy”) + verbalizing suffix む (-mu).
Ultimately derived the same as above, but generally regarded as a shortening of the longer phrase お休みなさい (oyasumi nasai, “good night”).

headline: The card has two Japanese cousins: カルタ and カルテ.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English card.
Doublet of カルタ (karuta, “traditional Japanese playing cards”) and カルテ (karute, “patient card”).
From English curd.

headline: “National language” also means Mandarin — but only in a Taiwanese sense.

sources.quote: From 国 (koku, “nation”) + 語 (go, “language”). The sense of "Mandarin" is derived from Taiwanese usage of the identical Chinese word 國語／国语 (guóyǔ).

headline: “Very young” may once have meant “without a chief”.

sources.quote: Possibly from Old Japanese. Japanese dictionaries cite the word to the Nihon Shoki (720), but only where kana glosses read 不賢 (literally “not mature; not capable”) as ヲサナシ (wosanasi). The first actual phonetic attestation is in the Shinsen Jikyō (898-901), as 乎佐奈志.
Compound of 長 (osa, “chief, senior”) + 無い (nai, “not”, from classical 無し (nashi)).

headline: “Grandmother” came from Chinese — but the ぼ in it is a change that happened inside Japanese.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 祖母 (MC tsuX muwX). Uses the kan'yōon for the 母 character, indicating a sound change within the Japanese language.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: “English” came from Chinese, or was assembled in Japan from “England” and “language”.

sources.quote: Borrowed from Chinese 英語 /英语 (Yīngyǔ), or a compound coined in Japan of 英(えい) (ei, “England”) + 語(ご) (-go, “language”).

headline: “One person” has a look-alike in Old Japanese: pi1dari, which became hidari.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese.
Derived from 一 (hito, “one, 1”) + 人 (-ri, counter for persons).
Compare Old Japanese 一人 (pi₁dari → hidari).

headline: “Wife” began, in Chinese, as a woman of the “room, chamber”.

sources.quote: Probably ultimately from Middle Chinese 女房 (MC nrjoX bjang), with an initial meaning in line with the spelling: 女 (woman) + 房 (“room, chamber”). First cited to 985.
* /njoːboː/ → /njoːbo/
Shortening of the final vowel in 女房 (nyōbō).
First cited to 1752.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Canned food is a “can stuffing”, with the つめ voicing to づめ.

sources.quote: From 缶(かん) (kan, “can”) + 詰(つ)め (tsume, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 詰(つ)める (tsumeru, “to stuff”).). The tsume changes to zume as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: A bar owner and a master of arts are the same English word — with an Italian twin.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English master. Doublet of マエストロ (maesutoro).

headline: “Temperature” is “warm” plus “degree”, and it appears in a text of 1837–1847.

sources.quote: Compound of 温(おん) (on, “warm”) + 度(ど) (do, “degree”).
Appeared in 舎密開宗 (Seimi Kaisō) of 1837-1847.

headline: A parcel is a “little package”, with つつみ voiced to づつみ.

sources.quote: Compound of 小(こ) (ko, “little”) + 包(つつ)み (tsutsumi, “package”). The tsutsumi changes to zutsumi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
